title: Forgiveness, Feasting, and the Lord of the Sabbath
summary: Back in Capernaum, Jesus forgives and heals a paralyzed man lowered through a roof, provoking scribes who say only God can forgive sins. He calls Levi the tax collector and eats with tax collectors and sinners, explains why his disciples do not fast while the bridegroom is with them, and defends his disciples for picking grain on the Sabbath, declaring that the Son of Man is Lord of the Sabbath.
story:
Chapter 1 showed Jesus' authority over evil spirits and disease and ended with crowds pressing in from every quarter, so that he could no longer enter a town openly. Chapter 2 brings him back into Capernaum, and the story turns from acclaim to conflict. Religious teachers now watch Jesus closely and object to what he says and does: he claims to forgive sins, he keeps company with the wrong people, his disciples do not fast, and they break the Sabbath rules as the teachers understood them.

This chapter holds four of a series of five controversy stories that runs to 3:6, where the Pharisees and Herodians begin plotting to destroy him. Each story asks a question, most of them beginning with why, and each ends with a saying of Jesus that answers more than was asked. Very early in the Gospel the shadow of the cross falls across the story. In verse 20 Jesus speaks of the day the bridegroom will be taken away, and the charge of blasphemy first spoken here (verse 7) is the charge on which he will be condemned (14:64). The chapter also introduces the title Jesus prefers for himself, the Son of Man, twice, both times with a claim to authority that belongs to God.
historical:
The chapter is still set in Galilee in the late 20s AD under Herod Antipas. Galilee was not taxed directly by Roman officials in this period; Antipas collected his own revenues and paid what he owed to Rome. Tolls and duties on goods were farmed out to contractors who bid for the right to collect them, paid in advance, and then collected what they could through local agents. Capernaum lay on the road near the Jordan, where goods passed between Antipas's territory and that of his brother Philip to the east, a natural place for a toll booth (verse 14). Levi was probably one of these local agents. Such men were widely despised, both as collaborators with the ruling house and because the system invited extortion; John the Baptist told tax collectors to collect no more than they were ordered (Luke 3:12-13). The Mishnah allows a person to make a false vow to escape murderers, robbers, and toll collectors (Nedarim 3:4), and it rules that a house becomes unclean if toll collectors enter it (Tohorot 7:6). Those texts are later than the Gospels, but they show how low the trade stood. Levi son of Alphaeus is called Matthew in the parallel (Matthew 9:9), and the church has usually taken the two names for one man.

The scribes were trained experts in the law of Moses who copied, taught, and applied it; Mark's phrase ‘the scribes of the Pharisees’ (verse 16, in the earliest manuscripts) names scribes who belonged to that party. The Pharisees were a lay movement devoted to the careful keeping of the law in daily life, especially purity, tithing, and the Sabbath. Josephus says they handed on to the people regulations received from the fathers that were not written in the law of Moses (Antiquities 13.297), the ‘tradition of the elders’ Mark will discuss in chapter 7. Their concerns were serious attempts to be faithful, and their questions in this chapter are the questions of observant people. Scholars debate how many Pharisees lived in Galilee at this time; Mark also describes scribes who came down from Jerusalem (3:22, 7:1). John's disciples (verse 18) remained a distinct group while their teacher was in prison and after his death; Acts still finds disciples who knew only John's baptism in Ephesus a generation later (Acts 19:1-7).

The story Jesus cites in verses 25 and 26 is told in 1 Samuel 21:1-6. Fleeing Saul, David came to the sanctuary at Nob and asked the priest for bread; the only bread on hand was the Bread of the Presence, and the priest gave it to him after asking whether David's men had kept themselves from women. The priest named there is Ahimelech. His son Abiathar escaped when Saul massacred the priests of Nob (1 Samuel 22:20), joined David, and served as his high priest for decades, which made him the better-known figure. The Babylonian Talmud reasons that David's visit fell on a Sabbath, since the old loaves were replaced with fresh ones on that day (Menahot 95b, from Leviticus 24:8); if Jesus' hearers knew that tradition, the precedent was even closer than it looks.
cultural:
Village houses in Galilee were built of basalt with flat roofs of wooden beams covered with branches and packed earth, often reached by an outside stair. Digging through such a roof (verse 4 uses verbs for unroofing and digging out) was possible, though it would have left a mess for the owner below. Luke, writing for readers who knew tiled roofs, says the man was let down ‘through the tiles’ (Luke 5:19). The paralyzed man lay on a mat or pallet (krabattos), a poor person's bedding, not a bed with legs. Many in Jesus' world assumed a link between sickness and sin. The disciples in John 9:2 ask “who sinned, this man or his parents,” and the Babylonian Talmud records Rabbi Ammi's saying that there is no suffering without iniquity (Shabbat 55a), though the same passage goes on to refute it. Jesus' first words to the man touch that assumption, and his later teaching refuses the simple equation (John 9:3).

Meals were eaten reclining on couches or mats, and to eat with someone was to accept them. Sinners in the Gospels names people known for disregarding the law or whose way of life put them outside the circle of the observant, including those in despised trades. For a teacher to share a table with them risked his reputation and, in the eyes of some, his purity. Jesus answers with a proverb about physicians that was common coin in the ancient world: Diogenes Laertius reports that the philosopher Antisthenes, criticized for keeping bad company, replied that physicians attend the sick without catching the fever (Lives of the Philosophers 6.6).

The law of Moses commanded only one annual fast, on the Day of Atonement, when Israel was to ‘afflict’ or humble itself (Leviticus 16:29-31), and the prophets knew other fasts that arose after the exile (Zechariah 8:19). Devout Jews added voluntary fasts: the Pharisee in Luke 18:12 fasts twice a week, and the early Christian manual called the Didache (8:1) tells believers not to fast on Monday and Thursday as the hypocrites do but on Wednesday and Friday, which suggests that twice-weekly fasting on those days was a known custom. John's disciples may have been fasting in repentance, in expectation, or in mourning for their imprisoned teacher. Fasting was unthinkable at a wedding. Wedding celebrations could last a week (Judges 14:12), and the ‘guests of the bridegroom’ (literally ‘sons of the bridal chamber’, a Semitic idiom) were the groom's companions whose duty was to celebrate.

The images in verses 21 and 22 come from the household. Cloth that had not been fulled (agnaphos, unshrunk) would shrink the first time it was washed and tear away from the older fabric around it. Wine was stored in goatskins, and fermenting new wine gave off gas and stretched its container; a new skin could stretch with it, but an old one, already stretched and hardened, would burst. The Sabbath, the seventh day, was set apart for rest (Exodus 20:8-11), and teachers defined which activities counted as work. The Mishnah later lists thirty-nine main categories of forbidden work, including reaping and threshing (Shabbat 7:2), and plucking and rubbing heads of grain could be classed under them. Deuteronomy 23:25 allowed a traveler to pluck grain by hand from a neighbor's field on an ordinary day. The Damascus Document from Qumran set out an even stricter Sabbath code (CD 10:14-11:18). The consecrated bread was the twelve loaves set out each Sabbath before the Lord in the sanctuary, which the law assigned to the priests to eat in a holy place (Leviticus 24:5-9).
literary:
The chapter contains four of the five controversy stories that run from 2:1 to 3:6. Each has a similar shape: an action by Jesus or his disciples, an objection, and a decisive saying from Jesus, often in the form of a proverb or a question. Joanna Dewey, in Markan Public Debate (1980), argued that the five are arranged concentrically. The first and last are healings in which Jesus' authority is questioned and his opponents think or keep silent in their hearts (2:1-12, 3:1-6). The second and fourth involve eating and are answered with sayings about Jesus' purpose and David (2:13-17, 2:23-28). The central story, about fasting, contains the first hint of Jesus' death (2:20). The series also escalates: the scribes object silently in their hearts (2:6), then question the disciples (2:16), then Jesus is questioned about his disciples (2:18), then he is questioned directly (2:24), and finally his opponents watch him to accuse him and go out to plot his death (3:2, 3:6).

The healing of the paralytic is itself a small sandwich, one of the arrangements James R. Edwards studied in Novum Testamentum (1989): a healing story (verses 1 to 5 and 11 and 12) enfolds a controversy about forgiveness (6 to 10), so that each explains the other. Verse 10 breaks off in the middle of a sentence as Jesus turns from the scribes to the man, a break the BSB marks with an ellipsis. The question ‘why’ (tí) drives the chapter: why does this man speak like this (7), why do you think these things (8), why does he eat with tax collectors (16), why do your disciples not fast (18), why are they doing what is unlawful (24). Jesus answers with images from ordinary life (a doctor, a wedding, a patch, a wineskin) and with Scripture (David), and each answer ends in a claim about himself: the Son of Man has authority to forgive, he came to call sinners, he is the bridegroom, and he is Lord of the Sabbath.

The two uses of Son of Man in the chapter (verses 10 and 28) are the first in Mark, and both come with a claim to authority, on earth and over the Sabbath. Mark will use the title fourteen times in all, and after chapter 8 it is joined almost always to suffering and to future glory.

outline.t: A paralyzed man forgiven and healed
Levi called; Jesus eats with sinners
The question about fasting: bridegroom, patch, and wineskins

doctrines.note: Jesus declares a man's sins forgiven before he heals his body, showing that forgiveness is the deeper need, and he says he came to call not the righteous but sinners (verse 17). Forgiveness here is God's free act, spoken with authority, and it comes before any sign of change in the man; the call to Levi shows the turning that follows.

The scribes are right that only God can forgive sins. Jesus does not deny it; he shows that the Son of Man, the figure of Daniel 7:13-14 who receives authority from God, has that authority on earth. He also names himself the bridegroom, a role Scripture gives to the LORD in his covenant love for Israel, and Lord of the Sabbath.

Jesus does not abolish the Sabbath but restores its purpose: “The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath” (verse 27). The day of rest was God's gift for human good, and its keeping should serve life and need, as the law itself allowed in David's case. Christians have drawn different conclusions from this for the Lord's Day, but all have read it as a word against using the Sabbath to deny mercy.

The chapter shows Jesus reading the law by its purpose and by Scripture, not setting it aside. He sends no one to break it, appeals to a precedent within Scripture, and claims authority over its application. The sayings about new wine and new skins suggest that what he brings cannot simply be added to the old patterns of observance.

“When Jesus saw their faith” (verse 5) is the first mention of faith in Mark. It is visible in what four men do, carrying their friend and digging through a roof, and it is the faith of friends as well as of the man himself. Mark's faith is trust that acts, and it comes to Jesus for what only he can give.

words.note: Aphiēmi, to release, let go, leave, forgive. It occurs about 143 times in the New Testament, often in the plain sense of leaving (the fishermen ‘left’ their nets in 1:18) and often for forgiving a debt or a sin. BDAG treats forgiveness as the cancellation of a debt or guilt. In verse 5 Jesus uses a present passive, ‘are forgiven’, which many read as a divine passive, pointing to God as the one who forgives; the scribes hear it as Jesus claiming to do what only God does, and Jesus confirms that reading in verse 10.

Huios, son, here in the phrase ho huios tou anthrōpou, the Son of Man. The phrase occurs about eighty times in the Gospels, almost always on Jesus' lips, and fourteen times in Mark, first in verses 10 and 28 of this chapter. In Hebrew and Aramaic ‘son of man’ can simply mean a human being (Psalm 8:4, Ezekiel 2:1), and Geza Vermes argued that Aramaic bar nasha could be a modest way of saying ‘I’. But Daniel 7:13-14 describes ‘One like the Son of Man’ to whom God gives dominion and authority (exousia in the Greek), and Mark's pairing of the title with authority in both verses points to Daniel's figure.

Hamartōlos, sinner. It occurs forty-seven times in the New Testament and six times in Mark, four of them in this chapter (15, 16 twice, 17). In the Gospels it often labels a social group, people seen as openly disregarding the law, and it is frequently paired with tax collectors. Jesus accepts the label as a description of those he came to call and refuses it as a reason to keep away.

Telōnēs, tax or toll collector. It occurs twenty-one times in the New Testament, all in the first three Gospels, and three times in Mark, all here (verses 15 and 16). The word names the local collectors of tolls and duties rather than the wealthy contractors above them. In Jesus' sayings the tax collector is a byword for the outsider (Matthew 5:46, 18:17), which makes his welcome of them all the more striking.

Numphios, bridegroom. It occurs sixteen times in the New Testament and three times in this chapter (verses 19 and 20). The Old Testament pictures the LORD as Israel's husband (Isaiah 54:5, 62:5; Hosea 2:19-20), and John the Baptist calls Jesus the bridegroom in John 3:29. By calling himself the bridegroom Jesus claims a role Scripture gives to God, and by saying the bridegroom will be ‘taken from them’ (the verb apairō, which the New Testament uses only in this saying and its parallels in Matthew and Luke) he hints at a violent removal.

Nēsteuō, to fast. It occurs twenty times in the New Testament and six times in verses 18 to 20. Fasting in Scripture expresses mourning, repentance, and urgent prayer. Jesus does not reject it; he says that his presence makes this a time of celebration like a wedding, and that his disciples will fast when he is taken away (verse 20), a saying the early church took as warrant for its own fasts (Didache 8:1).

Sabbaton, Sabbath, from Hebrew shabbat, the seventh day of rest. It occurs sixty-eight times in the New Testament and twelve times in Mark, five in verses 23 to 28. The Sabbath was a sign of the covenant between God and Israel (Exodus 31:13-17), a weekly remembrance of creation (Exodus 20:11) and of freedom from slavery (Deuteronomy 5:15). The plural form can mean simply a week, as in 16:2.

Blasphēmeō, to slander, to speak against God. It occurs thirty-four times in the New Testament and four times in Mark (2:7, 3:28, 3:29, 15:29). In the law blasphemy was speaking against the name of God and carried the death penalty (Leviticus 24:15-16); the Mishnah later narrowed the capital offense to pronouncing the divine name itself (Sanhedrin 7:5). The scribes use it broadly for claiming a prerogative that belongs to God, and the same charge will condemn Jesus at his trial (14:64).

christ:
The chapter shows Jesus doing what Israel's Scriptures reserve for God. “Who can forgive sins but God alone?” (verse 7), the scribes ask, and they have Scripture on their side: the LORD proclaims himself the one ‘forgiving iniquity, transgression, and sin’ (Exodus 34:7), and Isaiah 43:25 has God say, “I, yes I, am He who blots out your transgressions for My own sake.” Priests declared forgiveness through the sacrifices, and prophets announced it, as Nathan did to David (2 Samuel 12:13), but no one in the Old Testament forgives sins in his own name. Psalm 103:3 praises the LORD as the one “who forgives all your iniquities and heals all your diseases,” and in verse 11 Jesus does both, making the visible healing the proof of the invisible forgiveness.

He then names himself three ways. He is the physician who came for the sick, recalling the LORD who says “I am the LORD who heals you” (Exodus 15:26). He is the bridegroom, the role Scripture gives to God in his covenant love (Isaiah 62:5, Hosea 2:19-20), and his presence makes this a wedding feast, the image the prophets used for the joy of the coming age. And he is the Son of Man who is Lord even of the Sabbath, the day God himself made holy at creation. His appeal to David places him in David's line and claims more than David: the king's need could override the rule about holy bread, and the Son of Man has authority over the Sabbath itself.

The authority is exercised in mercy. It is used for a paralyzed man, at a table full of tax collectors, and on behalf of hungry disciples. Yet the chapter also looks toward the cost of that mercy. The bridegroom will be ‘taken from them’ (verse 20), the first hint of the death Mark will describe, and the charge of blasphemy spoken silently here will be spoken aloud at the trial where the Son of Man claims to sit at God's right hand (14:62-64). The one who forgives sins on earth will secure that forgiveness by giving his life ‘as a ransom for many’ (10:45).
interpretation:
Jewish tradition preserves close parallels to two sayings in this chapter. The Mekhilta of Rabbi Ishmael, an early rabbinic commentary on Exodus, records Rabbi Simeon ben Menasya (late second century) reading Exodus 31:14, “Keep the Sabbath, for it is holy to you,” to mean that the Sabbath is handed over to you, not you to the Sabbath; the Babylonian Talmud repeats it in a discussion of saving life on the Sabbath (Yoma 85b). The principle of verse 27 was at home in Jewish thought; the claim of verse 28 was not. On forgiveness, an Aramaic fragment from Qumran, the Prayer of Nabonidus (4Q242), tells of a Babylonian king healed after an exorcist, a Jew, forgave his sin, though the broken text may mean that God forgave; Daniel Johansson (Journal for the Study of the New Testament, 2011) surveyed early Jewish sources and concluded that forgiveness was everywhere treated as God's prerogative, mediated by priests and intercessors, while Tobias Hägerland (Jesus and the Forgiveness of Sins, 2012) argued that Jesus' forgiving belongs among the acts of a prophet declaring God's pardon.

The church fathers read the paralytic as a revelation of who Jesus is. Irenaeus (Against Heresies 5.17.2-3, around 180) argued that the one who said ‘your sins are forgiven’ was the Word of God against whom humanity first sinned, who became Son of Man and forgave as both God and man. Later writers drew moral lessons from the four friends, who became a standing image of intercessory love. In the Orthodox churches Mark 2:1-12 is the Gospel of the Second Sunday of Great Lent, the Sunday of Saint Gregory Palamas, and preachers there have read the paralytic as the soul turned back to God. The call of Levi and the meal with sinners became a model of the church's welcome. When Paolo Veronese painted a vast Last Supper for the Dominicans of Santi Giovanni e Paolo in Venice in 1573, crowded with soldiers, dwarfs, and dogs, the Inquisition summoned him to explain the irreverence; he retitled it The Feast in the House of Levi, a scene in which the Gospels say sinners were present. Caravaggio's Calling of Saint Matthew (1599 to 1600, Contarelli Chapel, Rome) paints the parallel call as a shaft of light across a tax collector's counting table.

The Sabbath sayings shaped Christian debate about the Lord's Day for centuries. Luther's Large Catechism (1529) taught that Christians are free from the literal seventh day and keep a day of rest so that servants may rest and all may hear God's word. The Westminster Confession (1647, chapter 21) taught a Christian Sabbath on the first day, kept in rest and worship, with room for works of necessity and mercy, a principle drawn from passages like this one. Seventh-day Christians have read the same chapter as confirming that Jesus kept the Sabbath while correcting its misuse. Modern scholars have asked what the disputes meant in their Jewish setting. Geza Vermes (Jesus the Jew, 1973) read Jesus as a Galilean holy man within Judaism, and E. P. Sanders (Jesus and Judaism, 1985) argued that disagreements over the Sabbath and food were the kind of debate observant Jews had among themselves and unlikely by themselves to lead to a death plot. Joanna Dewey's study of the chiastic design of 2:1-3:6 (1980) shaped how the whole section is taught.

In art, one of the earliest surviving pictures of Jesus anywhere is the healing of a paralytic on the wall of the house-church baptistery at Dura-Europos in Syria, about AD 232, now at Yale; it shows the man lying on his bed and then walking off with it, though whether it depicts this story or the similar healing in John 5 is uncertain. In the Revised Common Lectionary, Year B, verses 1 to 12 are read on the Seventh Sunday after the Epiphany, verses 13 to 22 on the Eighth, and 2:23-3:6 on the Ninth Sunday after the Epiphany or in early summer (Proper 4).
text:
Several differences between English Bibles in this chapter come from the manuscripts. In verse 16 the earliest manuscripts read ‘the scribes of the Pharisees’, an unusual phrase, while the text behind the King James Version reads the smoother ‘scribes and Pharisees’; the unusual phrase is probably original. In verse 17 the King James Version adds ‘to repentance’ after ‘sinners’, following later manuscripts that brought Mark into line with Luke 5:32; the earlier manuscripts lack it. In verse 5 some manuscripts read a perfect, ‘have been forgiven’ (the form in Luke 5:20), where the better-attested present says ‘are forgiven’. In verse 14 Codex Bezae and some other witnesses read ‘James son of Alphaeus’ instead of Levi, probably because a scribe noticed that Mark's list of the Twelve (3:18) has a James son of Alphaeus and no Levi. In verse 22 the last clause, “Instead, new wine is poured into new wineskins”, is missing from Codex Bezae and some Old Latin manuscripts.

Verse 26 has both a textual and a translation question. The phrase about Abiathar is missing from Codex Bezae, Codex Washingtonianus, and some Latin and Syriac witnesses, which may show that ancient copyists felt the difficulty discussed below; the best manuscripts include it, and all modern editions print it. The Greek epi Abiathar archiereōs can be rendered ‘when Abiathar was high priest’ (NIV, BSB ‘during the high priesthood of Abiathar’), ‘in the time of Abiathar the high priest’ (ESV), or, on John Wenham's proposal, ‘in the passage about Abiathar’, and the choice affects how the difficulty is solved. Verse 15 is ambiguous in Greek: the clause ‘for there were many who followed Him’ may describe the disciples or the tax collectors and sinners, and translations differ in their punctuation.

teach.big: Jesus exercises God's own authority to forgive, welcome, and restore, and that authority, which sets the old patterns of religion under new wine, is already moving him toward the cross where the bridegroom will be taken away.

outline.t: Faith is visible in what four friends do to bring a man to Jesus, and Jesus meets the need beneath the obvious one: the man's sins are forgiven.
The scribes rightly say only God forgives; Jesus proves that the Son of Man has that authority on earth by doing the thing they can see.
Jesus calls a despised toll collector and eats with sinners, because he came as a physician for the sick, not a judge of the healthy.
With Jesus present, it is a wedding, not a funeral; but the bridegroom will be taken away, and then his people will fast.
What Jesus brings cannot be patched onto old patterns; the new wine needs new skins.
The Sabbath was God's gift for human good, and the Son of Man, greater than David, is its Lord.

teach.pitfalls:
The most common misreading turns the Pharisees into villains and Jesus into an opponent of Jewish law. The Pharisees' questions are serious questions of faithful people, the Sabbath and fasting were God's own gifts, and Jesus appeals to Scripture and keeps the synagogue and the Sabbath himself. The contrast is not between Jewish legalism and Christian freedom but between observance cut off from its purpose and the arrival of the one who is its Lord. Teaching that caricatures Judaism fails the text and has done real harm.

A second pitfall is to make verses 1 to 12 a lesson that sickness is caused by personal sin. Jesus addresses the man's sins first, but he never says the paralysis was a punishment, and elsewhere he rejects that reasoning (John 9:3, Luke 13:1-5). A third turns verses 21 and 22 into a slogan for novelty in church life, so that anything new is justified by new wine; the new wine is the presence of Jesus and his kingdom, not a style of worship. A fourth treats verse 27 as permission to ignore rest altogether, when the saying affirms the Sabbath as a gift. Finally, resist building a doctrine of intercession on verse 5 alone; the faith of friends matters, but Mark does not explain how their faith relates to the man's own.
teach.pastoral: This chapter speaks to people who carry guilt and to those whose illness or disability has been blamed on their sin, sometimes by church people. Teach carefully that Jesus forgives the paralyzed man without suggesting that his condition was a punishment. It also speaks to people who feel they are too far outside the church to be welcome, such as the tax collectors of our day; Jesus eats with them before they have reformed. For those who are exhausted, verse 27 is good news: rest is God's gift, not a burden. And for those who cannot come to Jesus on their own, whether through illness, depression, or despair, the four friends show the church's calling to carry them.

hard.q: Jesus says David ate the consecrated bread when Abiathar was high priest, but 1 Samuel 21 names Ahimelech. Is this a mistake?
hard.a:
The objection is straightforward. In 1 Samuel 21:1-6 the priest at Nob who gives David the bread is Ahimelech; his son Abiathar becomes high priest only later. Matthew and Luke both leave the name out when they retell the story (Matthew 12:3-4, Luke 6:3-4), which suggests they noticed the problem, and some ancient scribes dropped it from Mark. Many critical scholars conclude that Mark or his source simply erred. Bart Ehrman, in Misquoting Jesus (2005), describes how a professor's comment on this verse, that perhaps Mark just made a mistake, helped unravel his belief that the Bible is without error, and the verse is often cited by skeptics for that reason.

Several answers have been offered. John Wenham (Journal of Theological Studies, 1950) argued that the Greek epi can mean ‘at the passage about’, as Mark 12:26 uses epi tou batou for ‘in the passage about the bush’; on this reading Jesus names the section of Samuel known by Abiathar, the story's most prominent priestly figure. Others read ‘in the days of Abiathar’, who was present at Nob, survived, and became the famous high priest of David's reign, not as a claim that he officiated that day. Others point out that the Old Testament itself mixes the names: 2 Samuel 8:17 names ‘Ahimelech son of Abiathar’ as David's priest, the reverse of the relationship in 1 Samuel, and 1 Chronicles 18:16 and 24:6 show the same confusion, so that Jesus or Mark may be following a tradition that used the names differently. Scholars who hold a high view of Scripture differ over which solution is best, and some of them grant that none is fully satisfying. The point of Jesus' argument, that Scripture itself shows human need and God's purpose standing behind the ceremonial law, is not affected by how the name is explained.

hard.q: Does Jesus claim to be God when he forgives the man's sins, or only to announce God's forgiveness as a prophet or priest might?
hard.a:
The strongest objection comes from Jewish and historical-critical readers. Priests pronounced forgiveness in God's name through the sacrifices (Leviticus 4:20), and prophets announced it (2 Samuel 12:13). The verb in verse 5 is passive, ‘your sins are forgiven’, which many take as a divine passive meaning ‘God forgives your sins’. On this reading Jesus declares God's pardon without claiming to be God, and the scribes' charge of blasphemy misunderstands him or is Mark's later framing. Tobias Hägerland (Jesus and the Forgiveness of Sins, 2012) argues that the historical Jesus forgave sins as a prophet, and Jewish scholars such as Geza Vermes read Jesus' words within the range of a Galilean holy man's authority. The Qumran Prayer of Nabonidus (4Q242), in which an exorcist may forgive a king's sin, is sometimes cited to show that such language was not unthinkable.

Other scholars answer that Mark's narrative makes a larger claim. Daniel Johansson (Journal for the Study of the New Testament, 2011) surveyed early Jewish sources and found no clear case of a human figure forgiving sins in his own right; intercessors and priests mediate a forgiveness that remains God's. In Mark, Jesus does not say that God has forgiven; he says the Son of Man ‘has authority on earth to forgive sins’ (verse 10), claims the prerogative the scribes assign to God alone, and does not correct their inference. Richard Hays and others read the scene with Jesus' later claims (the bridegroom, the Lord of the Sabbath, the Son of Man at God's right hand in 14:62) as part of Mark's portrait of Jesus sharing the identity of Israel's God. Irenaeus read it that way in the second century. Readers who hold that Jesus was a prophet and readers who confess him as God incarnate can agree that he spoke with an authority that astonished everyone present (verse 12); they differ on what that authority finally was, and Mark leaves the question pressing on his reader.

observe: Find every question in the chapter. Who asks each one, and how does Jesus answer?
What do the four friends do in verses 3 and 4, and what does Jesus see in it?
What images from ordinary life does Jesus use in verses 17 to 22?
interpret: Why does Jesus address the man's sins before his paralysis, and why is the healing called proof of the forgiveness?
What does Jesus mean by calling himself the bridegroom, and what is he hinting at in verse 20?
How does the story of David support the claim that the Sabbath was made for man, and what more does verse 28 claim?
apply: Who has carried you toward Jesus when you could not come yourself, and whom might you carry?
Whom would your church find it hardest to eat with, and what would Levi's table look like in your town?
Do you treat rest as a burden, a luxury, or a gift? What would receiving it as a gift change?
